text.p: These are the leading stories in the Namibian press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Deputy minister of Works, Transport and Communication Dr Klaus Dierks, deputy prime minister Hendrik Witbooi and the director of the Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit Henning Melber, have called for "labour intensive production" to combat unemployment in Namibia. During a workshop on job creation Dierks said his ministry had already put aside N$50 million, which in the next three years is to be spent on labour-intensive building and servicing projects. A draft whitepaper on the topic is being prepared by the ministry of Works, Transport and Communication.

- The debate around the third term for President Sam Nujoma has taken another turn with the national student organisation, Nacos, voicing its strongest objections against a change of the constitution for this purpose. Nacos has threatened with a strike of about half a million pupils and students, which could paralyse education in the country. The body says a change to the constitution to allow a third term for Nujoma is putting democracy in Namibia in jeopardy. Earlier the SWAPO elders council, the SWAPO Youth League, the Mine Workers Union and Prime Minister Hage Geingob had voiced their support for a change to the constitution in favour of a third term for the president ahead of the SWAPO congress scheduled for the end of this month.

- Telecom fears that two South Africans, who were granted bail of N$14 000 following their arrest on charges of theft of copperwire, will skip the country. Andy Lotter and his son Deon Lotter were arrested at Karibib after a large amount of copper wire, apparently stolen from Telcom lines, was found on their farm. Telcom's manager for the Windhoek region, Welbert Ockhuizen said on Thursday the company would do everything legally possible to have the bail revoked.
